content: State and local health department Childhood Lead Poisoning Prevention Programs (CLPPPs) must identify these high-risk areas and provide the necessary leadership to coordinate efforts aimed at eliminating these risks before children develop elevated blood lead levels (BLLs). Collaboration is critical among housing agencies, community development organizations, code enforcement bodies, elected officials, federal agencies, property owners, and community-based organizations to address lead hazards effectively. Expanding primary prevention initiatives will reduce the demand for secondary prevention services and improve their efficiency. However, since creating an adequate supply of lead-safe housing through primary prevention will take time, CLPPPs should supplement their systemic housing-based prevention programs with expedited initiatives to identify high-risk families who could benefit from immediate assessment and risk-reduction services. Other activities, like targeted code enforcement and community-based screening of high-risk housing, should focus on areas with the greatest lead hazards. In some cases, interventions may need to be applied at the level of individual properties, such as extending lead hazard control efforts from one apartment with a lead-poisoned child to other units in the same building with similar risks. Many of the activities described in this report will involve organizations beyond local health departments, including other public agencies, community groups, and private sector entities like property owners and lead-abatement contractors. Public health agencies must take the lead in educating stakeholders about lead safety and encouraging widespread action to create lead-safe housing. The report recommends eight foundational elements for a housing-based primary prevention program. Enhanced targeting strategies and information systems initially developed for improving lead screening in children should be used to direct resources toward reducing lead hazards in high-risk housing, particularly those occupied by low-income families with infants or expectant parents. Local jurisdictions must develop and enforce specific standards for lead-safe housing treatments, guided by EPA regulations and HUD guidelines. Local laws should require minimum lead-safe housing treatments for property repair and maintenance, tailored to the characteristics of the local housing stock, property risk, and rental market. For example, states like Maryland and Indiana mandate property owners to meet certain lead safety standards at key junctures, such as property turnover. Collaboration with housing and other relevant agencies is essential for completing the shift to primary prevention. While some aspects of secondary prevention programs will be retained, others may be redirected or deferred. Simultaneously, health education efforts could shift focus from general lead information to training contractors, property owners, and community members in lead-safe work practices. Jurisdictions receiving HUD Community Development Block Grant and HOME Housing Partnership funds are required to develop and annually update a Consolidated Plan that addresses lead hazards. This plan must estimate the number of housing units occupied by lowor moderate-income families that contain lead-based paint hazards and outline actions to evaluate and reduce these hazards. The plan should also describe how lead hazard reduction will be integrated into housing policies and programs and how public and private entities will coordinate efforts to enhance housing safety. CLPPPs should lead the development and use of benchmarks and milestones to track the progress of primary prevention efforts in their jurisdictions. Local data should guide decision-making, and creative partnerships will be necessary to evaluate prevention activities and outcomes. Systems for ongoing surveillance of children’s BLLs and the presence of lead hazards in housing will be critical for measuring progress. Additionally, CLPPPs should identify and promote research opportunities as part of their prevention efforts and plan robust evaluations to improve understanding of effective strategies.
